Alveolar macrophage (Dust cell phagocytosing particulate debris)
Club cells / Clara cells (Dome-shaped non-ciliated bronchiolar exocrine cells)
Type II Pneumocyte (Great alveolar cell)
explanation: Type II pneumocytes are cuboidal cells with apical microvilli and lamellar bodies that secrete pulmonary surfactant to lower alveolar surface tension and prevent end-expiratory atelectasis; they also divide to regenerate Type I cells.

questionText: The specialized venous vessels in the paracortex of lymph nodes lined by plump cuboidal endothelial cells that facilitate lymphocyte homing from the bloodstream are designated:
options: Trabecular veins
Sinusoids
High Endothelial Venules (HEVs)
Subcapsular sinuses
explanation: High Endothelial Venules (HEVs) in the paracortex have tall, plump, cuboidal endothelial cells expressing specific selectins and addressins that enable naive T and B lymphocytes in circulation to tether, roll, and extravasate into lymph node parenchyma.

questionText: In the developing mammalian embryo, the somites (derived from paraxial mesoderm) differentiate into three distinct cellular components: Sclerotome, Myotome, and Dermatome. The Sclerotome gives rise to:
options: Dermis of the dorsal trunk skin and subcutaneous connective tissue
The axial skeleton (vertebrae and ribs)
All skeletal musculature of the body trunk and limbs
Urogenital system (kidneys and gonads derived from intermediate mesoderm)
explanation: Paraxial mesoderm divides into somites; the ventromedial sclerotome cells migrate around the notochord and neural tube to form vertebrae, intervertebral discs, and ribs; myotome forms striated skeletal muscle; dermatome forms dorsal dermis.

questionText: Which extraordinary population of pluripotent embryonic cells arises from the neural fold margins during neurulation, migrating throughout the body to form melanocytes, Schwann cells, spinal and autonomic ganglia, and the adrenal medulla?
options: Neural Crest cells
Notochordal cells
Lateral plate mesoderm
Endodermal epithelial cells
explanation: Neural crest cells (often called the 'fourth germ layer') delaminate from neural folds, giving rise to peripheral sensory and autonomic ganglia, Schwann cells, melanocytes, craniofacial skeletal tissues, and adrenal medullary chromaffin cells.

questionText: In fetal circulation, the physiological vascular shunt that diverts oxygen-rich blood directly from the umbilical vein into the caudal vena cava, largely bypassing the fetal hepatic sinusoids, is the:
options: Urachus
Ductus venosus
Ductus arteriosus
Foramen ovale
explanation: The ductus venosus shunts approximately 50% of umbilical venous blood directly into the inferior (caudal) vena cava, bypassing the liver; postnatally, its fibrous remnant persists as the Ligamentum Venosum.

questionText: The adult anatomical remnant of the fetal 'Ductus Arteriosus' (which diverted pulmonary artery blood into the descending aorta) is the:
options: Ligamentum venosum
Ligamentum teres hepatis
Fossa ovalis
Ligamentum arteriosum
explanation: The ductus arteriosus connects the pulmonary artery to the descending aorta in the fetus; functional closure occurs at birth upon initiation of respiration, fibrosing into the adult Ligamentum Arteriosum (failure of closure results in Patent Ductus Arteriosus / PDA).

questionText: The adult anatomical remnant of the embryonic Left Umbilical Vein, running in the free margin of the falciform ligament to the visceral surface of the liver, is the:
options: Median umbilical ligament (Fibrous urachal remnant on ventral abdominal wall)
Ligamentum arteriosum (Fibrous remnant of the ductus arteriosus)
Ligamentum teres hepatis (Round ligament of the liver)
Ligamentum venosum (Fibrous remnant of the ductus venosus)
explanation: The round ligament of the liver (Ligamentum teres hepatis) is the fibrous obliterated remnant of the embryonic left umbilical vein, transporting oxygenated blood from placenta to fetus during gestation.

questionText: During embryonic gastrulation, the epithelial lining of the gastrointestinal tract, liver parenchyma, gall bladder, pancreas, and respiratory tree develops from which primary germ layer?
options: Endoderm
Neural crest
Ectoderm
Mesoderm
explanation: The endoderm forms the epithelial lining of the entire digestive canal (except stomodeum and proctodeum), the parenchyma of liver and pancreas, and the epithelial lining of the respiratory tract, urinary bladder, and urethra.

questionText: In male mammalian embryology, the primordial embryonic duct system that regresses under the influence of Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH / MIS) secreted by fetal Sertoli cells is the:
options: Mesonephric duct (Wolffian duct forming epididymis and deferent duct)
Paramesonephric duct (Müllerian duct)
Metanephric diverticulum (Ureteric bud forming renal collecting tubules)
Pronephric duct (Transient non-functional cranial embryonic pronephros)
explanation: In male embryos, Sertoli cells produce AMH, causing regression of the paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts (which would otherwise form uterine tubes, uterus, and cranial vagina), while testosterone supports Wolffian ducts to form epididymis and deferent ducts.

questionText: In the domestic fowl (Gallus domesticus), the fusion of the second to fifth thoracic vertebrae into a rigid dorsal bony unit to stabilize the trunk during flight is called the:
options: Notarium (Os dorsale)
Pygostyle
Synsacrum
Furcula
explanation: The notarium (os dorsale) is formed by the fusion of thoracic vertebrae T2 to T5 in the chicken, providing a rigid anchor for the thoracic cage and wing action, separated from the synsacrum by a single mobile thoracic vertebra (T6).

questionText: The 'Synsacrum' of birds is a rigid skeletal complex formed by the extensive fusion of which vertebral regions with the pelvic ilium?
options: Cervical and thoracic vertebrae
Caudal coccygeal vertebrae only
Sacral vertebrae alone
The last thoracic (T7), all lumbar, all sacral, and the first few caudal vertebrae
explanation: The avian synsacrum is formed by the complete bony fusion of the last thoracic vertebra, all lumbar vertebrae, all primary sacral vertebrae, and the cranial caudal (coccygeal) vertebrae, fusing seamlessly with the ilium of the pelvis.

questionText: The terminal fused caudal vertebrae in birds, shaped like a ploughshare and supporting the tail flight feathers (rectrices) and uropygial gland, is designated the:
options: Synsacrum
Furcula
Pygostyle
Notarium
explanation: The pygostyle consists of the fusion of the last 4 to 6 caudal coccygeal vertebrae, supporting the tail retrices (flight steering feathers) and providing an anchor for tail musculature and the preen gland.

questionText: The 'Triosseal Canal' (Foramen triosseum) of the avian pectoral girdle, through which the tendon of the Supracoracoideus muscle passes to act as a pulley for wing elevation, is formed by the junction of:
options: Scapula, Coracoid, and Clavicle
Sternum, Ribs, and Coracoid
Ilium, Ischium, and Pubis
Humerus, Radius, and Ulna
explanation: The triosseal canal is bounded by the scapula, coracoid, and clavicle; the tendon of the deep supracoracoideus muscle traverses this canal over the shoulder joint to insert on the dorsal humerus, functioning as a pulley to raise the wing (upstroke).

questionText: The 'Furcula' (popularly known as the 'wishbone') in birds is formed by the ventral midline fusion of the:
options: Two Coracoid bones (struts bracing the shoulder against sternum)
Two Scapulae (sword-like blade bones dorsal to the rib cage)
Costal cartilages (Sternal and asternal rib cartilaginous connections)
Right and Left Clavicles (along with the interclavicle)
explanation: The furcula is formed by the fusion of the left and right clavicles at their ventral ends, acting as an elastic spring during wing flapping to maintain spacing between shoulder joints.

questionText: In domestic poultry, the massive breast muscle responsible for the powerful downstroke of the wing during flight is the:
options: Biceps brachii muscle (Flexor of the antebrachium across the elbow joint)
Latissimus dorsi muscle (Superficial dorsal muscle retracting wing)
Pectoralis muscle (Pectoralis major / Pectoralis superficialis)
Supracoracoideus muscle (Deep pectoral causing the wing upstroke)
explanation: The Pectoralis (pectoralis major) originates from the ventral keel of the sternum and clavicle and inserts on the deltopectoral crest of the humerus, providing the main power for the downstroke; the Supracoracoideus elevates the wing.

questionText: In birds, the primary vocal organ responsible for sound production is situated at the bifurcation of the trachea into the primary bronchi and is termed the:
options: Larynx (which lacks vocal cords)
Syrinx
Tracheal bulb
Pharynx
explanation: The syrinx is the avian voice organ located at the caudal end of the trachea at the bronchial bifurcation, containing vibrating tympanic membranes (membrana tympaniformis) and syringeal muscles; the cranial avian larynx lacks vocal cords.

questionText: Avian lungs differ fundamentally from mammalian lungs because they are non-collapsible, constant-volume structures where gas exchange occurs in tubular:
options: Alveolar ducts and sacs terminating in respiratory bronchioles
Muscular trabeculae and visceral pleural sinuses without true gas exchange
Parabronchi (Air capillaries) with unidirectional airflow
Blind alveolar saccules with bidirectional tidal airflow
explanation: Avian lungs do not expand or collapse and lack dead-end alveoli; instead, inspired air flows unidirectionally through tertiary bronchi (parabronchi) and microscopic air capillaries that interlace with blood capillaries.

questionText: How many total air sacs (sacci pneumatici) are typically present in the domestic fowl (Gallus domesticus)?
options: 9 (1 single interclavicular, 2 cervical, 2 cranial thoracic, 2 caudal thoracic, and 2 abdominal)
7 (1 single clavicular, 2 cervical, 2 thoracic, and 2 paired caudal abdominal air sacs)
8 (2 clavicular, 2 cervical, 2 cranial thoracic, and 2 caudal abdominal air sacs)
12 (2 cervical, 4 thoracic, 2 axillary, 2 pelvic, and 2 caudal abdominal air sacs)
explanation: The domestic chicken has 9 air sacs: one unpaired Interclavicular air sac, and four paired air sacs (Cervical, Cranial Thoracic, Caudal Thoracic, and Abdominal); they act as bellows to drive unidirectional air through the lungs.

questionText: The thick muscular grinding stomach (gizzard / ventriculus) of the domestic fowl is lined internally by a tough, wear-resistant, yellowish-green protective cuticle termed:
options: Dense mucosal glycocalyx layer with high neutral mucin content
Koilin layer (composed of hardened protein secreted by mucosal tubular glands)
Enamel-like hydroxyapatite crystals embedded in fibrous connective tissue
Keratinized stratified squamous epithelium with stratum corneum
explanation: The gizzard lumen is protected by a tough koilin layer, a keratin-like polysaccharide-protein complex secreted by deep mucosal tubular glands that hardens upon exposure to hydrochloric acid from the proventriculus.

questionText: In the domestic fowl, the glandular stomach (Proventriculus) contains specialized mucosal cells that secrete both pepsinogen and hydrochloric acid, known as:
options: Parietal cells
Enterochromaffin cells
Chief cells
Oxynticopeptic cells
explanation: Unlike mammals which have distinct parietal (HCl) and chief (pepsinogen) cells, avian proventricular glands possess a single composite cell type: the Oxynticopeptic cell, which performs both secretory functions.

questionText: Prominent lymphoid aggregations located in the mucosal wall at the proximal origin (base) of each of the two ceca in the domestic fowl are designated:
options: Peyer's patches
Cecal tonsils
Harderian glands
Bursa of Fabricius
explanation: The cecal tonsils are major gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT) structures located at the ileocecal junctions at the proximal neck of both ceca, mounting mucosal immune responses against enteric pathogens.

questionText: The dorsal diverticulum of the cloacal proctodeum in young birds that serves as the primary site of B lymphocyte differentiation and lymphopoiesis is the:
options: Harderian gland
Thymus
Bursa of Fabricius (Cloacal bursa)
Cecal tonsil
explanation: The Bursa of Fabricius is a dorsal diverticulum opening into the proctodeum of the cloaca; it is the unique primary lymphoid organ where B-cell maturation and immunoglobulin gene conversion occur in young birds, undergoing involution at sexual maturity.

questionText: In the domestic hen, the segment of the functional left oviduct where the thick and thin albumen (egg white) is synthesized and secreted over approximately 3 hours is the:
options: Infundibulum
Isthmus
Uterus (Shell gland)
Magnum
explanation: The magnum is the longest and most glandular segment of the avian oviduct (approx. 33 cm), densely lined with tubular glands secreting ovalbumin, conalbumin, ovomucoid, and lysozyme around the vitelline membrane of the descending yolk.

questionText: In birds, the excretory system is characteristically devoid of which two anatomical structures that are otherwise universal in domestic mammals?
options: Renal pelvis and Urinary bladder
Ureters and Collecting ducts
Glomeruli and Proximal tubules
Renal cortex and Medulla
explanation: Birds lack both a renal pelvis and a urinary bladder; ureters transport a semi-solid paste of uric acid directly from the three-lobed kidneys to empty into the urodeum of the cloaca, minimizing weight for flight and conserving water.
